questions.question: Identify the conjugate base of the hydronium ion.
questions.answer: A conjugate base is formed when an acid donates a proton. $H_3O^+\to H^++H_2O$, so the conjugate base of $H_3O^+$ is $H_2O$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following compounds has the highest molar solubility in water at $25^\circ$C (use the $K_{sp}$ values from the data sheet)?
questions.answer: Using data sheet $K_{sp}$ values: $BaCO_3$ ($2.58\times10^{-9}$): $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}=5\times10^{-5}$ M. $Mg_3(PO_4)_2$ ($1.04\times10^{-24}$): $K_{sp}=108s^5$, $s=6\times10^{-6}$ M. $Pb(OH)_2$ ($1.43\times10^{-20}$): $K_{sp}=4s^3$, $s=1.5\times10^{-7}$ M. $CaSO_4$ ($4.93\times10^{-5}$): $s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}=7.0\times10^{-3}$ M. $CaSO_4$ has the highest molar solubility (D).

questions.question: The graph shows how the rates of the forward and reverse reactions, as shown by the balanced equations on the graph, change over time. Which of the following statements, from the data shown, is correct?
questions.answer: The reverse rate increases from zero as products ($N_2O_4$ is not present initially; $NO_2$ builds up) accumulate, and it reaches its highest value when it becomes equal to the forward rate at equilibrium (A). The graph gives rates, not concentrations, so B cannot be deduced. The forward reaction $N_2O_4\to2NO_2$ increases the number of moles of gas, so the pressure rises (not C). At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal, non-zero rates (not D).
options: At equilibrium, the reverse reaction proceeds at its maximum rate.
After 10 s, the concentration of $NO_2(g)$ would be double that of $N_2O_4(g)$.
The pressure in the reaction vessel would decrease over the first 10 seconds.
After 10 s, any chemical reactions between the gases in the vessel have ceased.

questions.question: The graph shows the change in colour of four different indicators over a pH range of 2 to 10. An unknown solution is tested with indicator $P$, which turns purple. A fresh sample is tested with indicator $R$, which turns red. The likely pH of the unknown solution is:
questions.answer: Indicator $P$ is purple above its transition range, which ends at about pH 5.5, so the pH is above about 5.5. Indicator $R$ is red below its transition range, which starts at about pH 6.5, so the pH is below about 6.5. Only pH 6 satisfies both (B).

questions.question: Consider the compound represented by the formula $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$. What is the name of this compound?
questions.answer: The $-CONH_2$ group is an amide. With three carbons (including the carbonyl carbon) the name is propanamide (D).

questions.question: The graph shows the relationship between $\Delta H$, $T\Delta S$ and temperature in a chemical system. At $T_1$ the $\Delta G$ for the reaction is
questions.answer: $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$. At $T_1$ ($\approx233$ K) the graph gives $\Delta H\approx-92$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ and $T\Delta S\approx-53$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, so $\Delta G\approx-92-(-53)=-39\approx-40$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (D). (At $T_2$ the lines cross and $\Delta G=0$.)

questions.question: Methane gas was reacted with oxygen in a closed container until the following equilibrium was achieved: $2CH_4(g)+O_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2CO(g)+4H_2(g)$, $\Delta H=-76$ kJ. Which alternative correctly predicts how the quantity of hydrogen gas could be increased?
questions.answer: There are 3 mol of gas on the left and 6 mol on the right. Decreasing the pressure favours the side with more moles of gas, so the equilibrium shifts right and more $H_2$ forms (B). A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic (reverse) direction for this exothermic reaction. The equilibrium constant changes only with temperature, and reducing $[CH_4]$ would shift the equilibrium left.
options: Decreasing the pressure of the system.
Increasing the temperature of the system.
Changing the equilibrium constant for the reaction by reducing the methane concentration.

questions.question: Ethanol is an alternative fuel to petrol. Consider the statements: I. Ethanol releases more energy per gram when completely combusted than petrol. II. Ethanol releases less $CO_2$ per mole of fuel combusted than petrol. III. Ethanol is less likely to undergo incomplete combustion than petrol. IV. Ethanol can be produced from non-fossil fuel resources. Which of the above statements correctly compares ethanol to petrol when used as a fuel?
questions.answer: I is false: petrol (octane and similar hydrocarbons) releases about 48 kJ g$^{-1}$ compared with about 30 kJ g$^{-1}$ for ethanol. II is true: ethanol ($C_2$) gives 2 mol $CO_2$ per mole, while petrol (about $C_8$) gives about 8. III is true: ethanol contains oxygen, so combustion is more complete. IV is true: ethanol can be made by fermentation of plant material (D).

questions.question: Cloudy ammonia is an ingredient of some household cleaners. It forms an equilibrium mixture when dissolved in water: $NH_3(aq)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons NH_4^+(aq)+OH^-(aq)$. Which of the following is the equilibrium expression for the forward reaction?
questions.answer: The equilibrium expression is products over reactants, omitting the liquid water: $K=\dfrac{[NH_4^+][OH^-]}{[NH_3]}$ (A).

questions.question: Which of the following statements best explains the cleaning action of soap?
questions.answer: Soap has a charged (ionic) hydrophilic head, which interacts with polar water through ion–dipole forces, and a non-polar hydrocarbon tail, which interacts with non-polar oils and fats through dispersion forces (D).
options: The polar head group forms dispersion forces with oils and fats and the non-polar tail group forms hydrogen bonds with water.
The non-polar tail group forms dispersion forces with oil and fats, as well as forming dipole–dipole forces with water.
The polar head group forms dipole–dipole forces with oil, fats and water.
The polar head group forms ion–dipole forces with water and the non-polar tail group forms dispersion forces with oil and fats.

questions.question:
Which of the following is correct about the laboratory production of alcohol by the process of fermentation?

| | Requires oxygen | Produces oxygen | Suitable temperature ($^\circ$C) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Yes | No | 60 |
| B | No | Yes | 60 |
| C | No | No | 30 |
| D | Yes | No | 30 |
questions.answer: Fermentation of glucose by yeast, $C_6H_{12}O_6\to2C_2H_5OH+2CO_2$, is anaerobic (no oxygen required) and produces $CO_2$, not $O_2$. The enzymes in yeast work best at about $30$–$37^\circ$C and are denatured at $60^\circ$C (C).
options: Requires oxygen: yes; produces oxygen: no; $60^\circ$C
Requires oxygen: no; produces oxygen: yes; $60^\circ$C
Requires oxygen: no; produces oxygen: no; $30^\circ$C
Requires oxygen: yes; produces oxygen: no; $30^\circ$C

questions.question: A chemist synthesises a substance using the following pathway: $X\xrightarrow{\text{hydration}}Y\xrightarrow{\text{oxidation}}Z$. What are compounds $X$, $Y$ and $Z$?
questions.answer: Hydration is the addition of water across a $C=C$ double bond, so $X$ must be an alkene (prop-1-ene), not propane. Following Markovnikov's rule, hydration of prop-1-ene gives mainly propan-2-ol ($Y$). Oxidation of the secondary alcohol propan-2-ol gives the ketone propan-2-one (propanone) ($Z$) and cannot give a carboxylic acid (C).

questions.question: The graph shows the progress of an equilibrium reaction (reactants $\rightleftharpoons$ products): concentration of reactants (dashed line) and products (solid line) against time. Which row of the table correctly identifies what is happening at $t_1$, $t_2$ and $t_3$?
questions.answer: At $t_1$ both concentrations are constant, so the system is at equilibrium. At $t_2$ the concentration of the reactants suddenly jumps up and then falls, while the concentration of products rises to a higher level: reactants have been added and the system responds by shifting to the right. By $t_3$ the concentrations are constant again at a new equilibrium position (A).
options: $t_1$: at equilibrium; $t_2$: reactants added; $t_3$: new equilibrium position
$t_1$: at equilibrium; $t_2$: products added; $t_3$: new equilibrium position
$t_1$: no reaction occurring; $t_2$: reaction proceeding; $t_3$: reaction occurring
$t_1$: only forward reaction occurring; $t_2$: forward and reverse reactions occurring; $t_3$: only reverse reaction occurring

questions.question: The energy profile for the equilibrium reaction $2NO_2(g)\rightleftharpoons N_2O_4(g)$ is shown. The activation energies of the forward and reverse directions are
questions.answer: The activation energy of the forward reaction is the energy difference from the reactants ($2NO_2$ at about $0$) to the top of the peak (about $116$ kJ mol$^{-1}$). The reverse activation energy is the difference from the products ($N_2O_4$, at about $-60$ kJ mol$^{-1}$) to the peak: $116-(-60)=176$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (C).
options: Forward: 50 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$
Forward: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 50 kJ mol$^{-1}$
Forward: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 176 kJ mol$^{-1}$
Forward: 176 kJ mol$^{-1}$; reverse: 116 kJ mol$^{-1}$

questions.question: The structural formulae of five organic compounds, labelled A–E, are shown (A is methyl propanoate, B is ethyl ethanoate, C is 2-methylpropanoic acid, D is propyl methanoate and E is butanoic acid). Which alternative below identifies a pair of these compounds as examples of each type of isomer?
questions.answer: Functional group isomers have the same molecular formula but different functional groups: C (a carboxylic acid) and D (an ester) are such a pair. Position isomers have the same functional group in a different position or arrangement: A (methyl propanoate) and B (ethyl ethanoate) are both esters with the ester linkage in a different position in the carbon chain (B). In the other options the first pair (C and E, A and B) are the same family, and B and C are not the same family.
options: Functional group isomers: C and E; position isomers: B and D
Functional group isomers: C and D; position isomers: A and B
Functional group isomers: A and B; position isomers: A and B
Functional group isomers: B and E; position isomers: B and C

questions.question: Alcohols can be produced in many ways. Which method identified below requires the use of a dilute acid catalyst to yield alcohol?
questions.answer: Hydration of an alkene, $C=C+H_2O\to C(H)-C(OH)$, is catalysed by a dilute acid such as $H_2SO_4$ or $H_3PO_4$ (D). Substitution reactions of haloalkanes need no acid catalyst, and fermentation uses the enzymes in yeast.
options: Substitution of a halogenated hydrocarbon with hydroxide ion
Substitution of a halogenated hydrocarbon with water

questions.question: Consider the equilibrium $N_2O_4(g)\rightleftharpoons2NO_2(g)$, for which $K_{eq}=0.48$ at $100^\circ$C. In an experiment it was found that the concentration of $N_2O_4(g)$ was $0.20$ mol L$^{-1}$. Calculate the concentration of the $NO_2(g)$ in this equilibrium mixture.
Compound X has the general formula $C_nH_{2n}$. The mass spectrum for compound X is shown. Compound X is
questions.answer: The molecular ion peak is at $m/z=84$, the molar mass of $C_6H_{12}$. Methane ($CH_4$, 16) and but-1-ene ($C_4H_8$, 56) do not fit, and 2,2-dimethylbutane is $C_6H_{14}$ (86) and has the formula $C_nH_{2n+2}$. Compound X is hex-1-ene (C), with typical alkene fragments at $m/z=41$, $42$, $55$ and $56$.

questions.question: The following incomplete equation describes the oxidation of ethanol to ethanoic acid by potassium permanganate. All coefficients shown are correct, but the coefficient for ethanoic acid has been replaced by the letter 'X': $3C_2H_5OH(l)+4KMnO_4(aq)\to X\,CH_3COOH(l)+4MnO_2(s)+4KOH(aq)+H_2O(l)$. In a reaction carried out by a chemist, $5.0$ g of ethanol yields $5.9$ g of ethanoic acid. What is the percentage yield for the above reaction, as predicted by the correctly balanced equation?
questions.answer: Balancing carbon gives $X=3$. $n(C_2H_5OH)=\frac{5.0}{46.07}=0.1085$ mol, so the theoretical $n(CH_3COOH)=0.1085$ mol (3:3) and $m=0.1085\times60.05=6.52$ g. Percentage yield $=\frac{5.9}{6.52}\times100=91\%$ (D).

questions.question: A quantity of solid silver nitrate is added to $150.0$ mL of $0.120$ mol L$^{-1}$ potassium sulfate at $25^\circ$C to produce a precipitate. What mass of silver nitrate is required to cause precipitation to start? ($K_{sp}(Ag_2SO_4)=1.20\times10^{-5}$)
questions.answer: The precipitate is $Ag_2SO_4$ with $K_{sp}=[Ag^+]^2[SO_4^{2-}]=1.20\times10^{-5}$. Precipitation starts when $[Ag^+]=\sqrt{\dfrac{1.20\times10^{-5}}{0.120}}=0.0100$ M. $n(AgNO_3)=0.0100\times0.1500=1.5\times10^{-3}$ mol and $m=1.5\times10^{-3}\times169.9=0.255$ g (C, $0.254$ g).

questions.question: Using IUPAC nomenclature, name the compounds shown below (Compound 1: $CH_3CH_2CH_2CONH_2$, Compound 2: $CH_3C\equiv CH$, Compound 3: $CH_3COOH$).
questions.answer: Compound 1: butanamide. Compound 2: propyne. Compound 3: ethanoic acid (acetic acid).

questions.question: Compound 1 is butanamide ($CH_3CH_2CH_2CONH_2$), Compound 2 is propyne ($CH_3C\equiv CH$) and Compound 3 is ethanoic acid ($CH_3COOH$). Predict the order of boiling points (lowest to highest) of these molecules.
questions.answer: Compound 2 < Compound 3 < Compound 1 (propyne < ethanoic acid < butanamide).

questions.question: Compound 1 is butanamide ($CH_3CH_2CH_2CONH_2$), Compound 2 is propyne ($CH_3C\equiv CH$) and Compound 3 is ethanoic acid ($CH_3COOH$). Their boiling points increase in the order Compound 2 < Compound 3 < Compound 1. Explain this order.
questions.answer: The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the higher the boiling point. Compound 2 (propyne) is non-polar and has only weak dispersion forces. Compound 3 (ethanoic acid) has weak dispersion forces plus the polar $-COOH$ group, which forms hydrogen bonds between the $O-H$ hydrogen of one molecule and an oxygen of a neighbouring molecule. Compound 1 (butanamide) also forms strong hydrogen bonds (between the $N-H$ hydrogens and the carbonyl oxygen), and it also has a larger mass and longer carbon chain than ethanoic acid, so its dispersion forces are stronger. It therefore has the highest boiling point.

questions.question: When ammonia gas ($NH_3$) is bubbled through water that contains a few drops of phenolphthalein indicator, the water turns pink. Explain how the Brønsted–Lowry theory of acids and bases can account for this observation. Support your response with a chemical equation.
questions.answer: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solutions and pink in basic solutions. According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, a base is a proton acceptor. When ammonia dissolves, it accepts a proton from water, forming $NH_4^+$ and leaving $OH^-$ ions: $NH_3(g)+H_2O(l)\rightleftharpoons NH_4^+(aq)+OH^-(aq)$. The excess of $OH^-$ ions raises the pH (the solution becomes basic, above about pH 8.3) and so the phenolphthalein turns pink.

questions.question:
A colourimeter with an orange filter was used to analyse the concentration of copper ions in a solution. To calibrate the colourimeter, a distilled water blank and five standards of $Cu^{2+}$ were prepared. Their absorbances were measured:

| Concentration (mol L$^{-1}$) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| $0.0000$ | $0.00$ |
| $0.0005$ | $0.10$ |
| $0.0010$ | $0.19$ |
| $0.0020$ | $0.35$ |
| $0.0025$ | $0.43$ |
| $0.0030$ | $0.51$ |

Graph the calibration curve on the grid provided.
questions.answer: Plot absorbance (vertical axis) against concentration of $Cu^{2+}$ in mol L$^{-1}$ (horizontal axis), with labelled axes including units, scales that use most of the grid (for example $0$ to $0.0035$ and $0$ to $0.6$), points plotted accurately, and a straight line of best fit through the points (it is close to the origin).

questions.question: A colourimeter with an orange filter was calibrated using standards of $Cu^{2+}$: absorbance $0.00$ at $0$, $0.10$ at $0.0005$ mol L$^{-1}$, $0.19$ at $0.0010$, $0.35$ at $0.0020$, $0.43$ at $0.0025$ and $0.51$ at $0.0030$ mol L$^{-1}$. A $20.0$ mL sample of a copper solution of unknown concentration was diluted to a total volume of $80.0$ mL. When analysed with the colourimeter this diluted solution recorded an absorbance of $0.46$. What is the concentration of the copper ions in the $20.0$ mL sample in ppm?
questions.answer:
From the calibration line, an absorbance of $0.46$ corresponds to $[Cu^{2+}]\approx0.0027$ mol L$^{-1}$ in the diluted solution. The dilution factor is $\frac{80.0}{20.0}=4$, so the original concentration is $0.0027\times4=0.0108$ mol L$^{-1}$. Mass per litre $=0.0108\times63.55=0.686$ g L$^{-1}=686$ mg L$^{-1}$. The concentration is about $6.9\times10^{2}$ ppm.

Note: a reading of $0.0027$ M is from the marking guide; a reading of about $0.00267$ M from the line of best fit gives about $680$ ppm, which is equally acceptable.

questions.question: Initially a 2.00 L vessel contains a mixture of 1.00 mol of colourless hydrogen gas and 1.00 mol of purple iodine gas. The gases react: $H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HI(g)$, $\Delta H=+26$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. A chemical analyst is monitoring the system. Describe how the analyst would qualitatively know the system has reached equilibrium.
questions.answer: The purple colour of the mixture stops changing (it remains a constant intensity), indicating that the concentrations of all species are constant.

questions.question: A 2.00 L vessel initially contains 1.00 mol of $H_2(g)$ and 1.00 mol of $I_2(g)$, which react: $H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HI(g)$. At $400^\circ$C equilibrium is reached and the concentration of $HI(g)$ is $0.760$ mol L$^{-1}$. Calculate the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
For the reaction $H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HI(g)$ at $400^\circ$C the equilibrium constant is calculated to be $40.1$. Describe what this equilibrium constant indicates about the reaction.
questions.answer: Since $K_{eq}\gg1$, the equilibrium lies to the right: products ($HI$) are favoured, so at equilibrium there is a much greater concentration of products than reactants.

questions.question: The reaction $H_2(g)+I_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2HI(g)$ has $\Delta H=+26$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Using Le Châtelier's principle, explain what would happen to the equilibrium if the temperature was increased, with all other conditions remaining the same.
questions.answer: The forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H$ positive). According to Le Châtelier's principle, when the temperature is increased the system shifts in the direction that opposes the change, i.e. that absorbs the extra heat. This is the endothermic forward reaction, so the equilibrium shifts to the right, producing more $HI$ (the equilibrium constant increases) until a new equilibrium is established.

questions.question: A student in a school laboratory performed a reaction using methanoic acid and pentan-1-ol. Draw (using full structural formulae) and name the products of the reaction between methanoic acid and pentan-1-ol.
questions.answer: This is an esterification (condensation) reaction: $HCOOH+CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2OH\rightleftharpoons HCOOCH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3+H_2O$. The products are pentyl methanoate (an ester, drawn as $H-C(=O)-O-CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3$ with all bonds and hydrogens shown) and water.

questions.question: A student performed a reaction using methanoic acid and pentan-1-ol using the following method: (1) $10$ mL of pentan-1-ol and $12$ mL of methanoic acid were added to a $50$ mL round-bottomed flask; (2) $1$ mL of concentrated sulfuric acid was added to the flask; (3) the mixture was heated under reflux (apparatus shown) for $30$ minutes. Justify this procedure to efficiently produce this ester in a school laboratory.
questions.answer: Reflux: heating increases the rate of the slow esterification reaction (more collisions with energy above the activation energy). The reflux condenser condenses the volatile reactants and product (and the flammable vapours) and returns them to the flask, so none is lost and heating can continue for 30 minutes safely. Anti-bumping chips ensure smooth boiling. Catalyst: concentrated sulfuric acid is a catalyst that provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, speeding up the reaction, so equilibrium is reached in a reasonable time. It is also a dehydrating agent, absorbing the water produced, which by Le Châtelier's principle shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases the yield. Excess reactant: the esterification is reversible, $RCOOH+R'OH\rightleftharpoons RCOOR'+H_2O$, with a small equilibrium constant. Methanoic acid is used in excess (about $0.32$ mol compared with about $0.09$ mol of the alcohol), which shifts the equilibrium to the right (Le Châtelier) and converts more of the alcohol to the ester. The heating is gentle (e.g. with a heating mantle or water bath, not an open flame) because the reactants are flammable.

questions.question: Write a balanced chemical equation for the complete combustion of butan-1-ol.
questions.answer: $C_4H_9OH(l)+6O_2(g)\to4CO_2(g)+5H_2O(l)$ (or $(g)$ for the water)

questions.question: Theoretically, how much heat is released when $1.00$ g of butan-1-ol is combusted? The molar heat of combustion of butan-1-ol is $-2676$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Experimentally, $40\%$ of the heat is lost to the environment when $1.00$ g of butan-1-ol ($36.1$ kJ released in theory) is burned. If $100$ mL of water, initially at $25^\circ$C, was heated by the burning of $1.00$ g of butan-1-ol, what is the final temperature of the water? (Specific heat capacity of water $=4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$; $1.00$ mL of water has a mass of $1.00$ g.)
questions.answer: Heat absorbed by the water $=60\%\times36.1=21.7$ kJ $=2.17\times10^4$ J. $q=mc\Delta T$: $\Delta T=\dfrac{2.17\times10^4}{100\times4.18}=51.8^\circ$C. Final temperature $=25+51.8\approx77^\circ$C.

questions.question: The combustion of butan-1-ol is considered a non-equilibrium system. Discuss why this is a non-equilibrium system with reference to enthalpy and entropy.
questions.answer: A system is at equilibrium only if it is closed and the forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. In a non-equilibrium system the reverse reaction does not occur to a significant extent and the reaction goes to completion. The combustion of butan-1-ol is exothermic ($\Delta H$ negative), which favours the forward reaction because it is energetically favourable for the system to release energy. The entropy change is positive (the system becomes more disordered) as one large molecule and oxygen are converted to a larger number of small molecules, $CO_2$ and $H_2O$ (and the heat and gas released disperse into the surroundings). Both enthalpy and entropy therefore favour the forward reaction, $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$ is always negative, and nothing favours the reverse reaction, so the reaction goes to completion and no equilibrium is established.

questions.question: A solution contains three cations: barium, lead and copper. The flow chart indicates the steps used to confirm the identity of these cations: the solution is treated with excess $HCl$ and filtered (precipitate 1, filtrate 1); filtrate 1 is treated with excess $H_2SO_4$ and filtered (precipitate 2, filtrate 2). Identify precipitate 1.
questions.answer: Precipitate 1 is lead(II) chloride, $PbCl_2$.

questions.question: A solution contains three cations: barium, lead and copper. The first step in a flow chart to confirm their identity is the addition of excess hydrochloric acid. Explain why $HNO_3$ is an inappropriate choice for the first step.
questions.answer: All nitrates are soluble, so $HNO_3$ would not precipitate any of the cations. It would not separate (distinguish) the ions, as $Pb^{2+}$ forms an insoluble precipitate with chloride but not with nitrate.

questions.question: A solution contains barium, lead and copper cations. Excess $HCl$ is added and the $PbCl_2$ precipitate is filtered off. Excess $H_2SO_4$ is then added to filtrate 1, forming precipitate 2, which is filtered off, leaving filtrate 2. Write a net ionic equation that represents the formation of precipitate 2.
questions.answer: Precipitate 2 is barium sulfate: $Ba^{2+}(aq)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\to BaSO_4(s)$.

questions.question: A solution contained barium, lead and copper cations. $PbCl_2$ was precipitated with excess $HCl$, and $BaSO_4$ with excess $H_2SO_4$. What colour would you expect filtrate 2 (which contains the remaining cation) to be?
questions.answer: Blue, due to the hydrated copper(II) ions, $[Cu(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$.

questions.question: Filtrate 2 contains the remaining cation, $Cu^{2+}$, after $Pb^{2+}$ and $Ba^{2+}$ have been precipitated. Describe an additional test you could conduct, and the expected results, that would confirm the identity of the cation in filtrate 2.
questions.answer: Flame test: dip a clean wire loop into the solution and hold it in a Bunsen flame; copper ions produce a green flame. Alternatively, add $NaOH$ solution to give a pale blue precipitate of $Cu(OH)_2$, or add excess ammonia solution, which gives a deep blue solution of $[Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}$.

questions.question: The Gunwinggu people of Arnhem Land eat the roots of a bitter yam plant, which contains toxic salts called oxalates. Using this, or another example, identify at least two steps used in the preparation of these foods and outline how these steps demonstrate chemical principles to make the food safe to eat.
questions.answer: Step 1: the yam roots are ground or pounded and soaked or leached in water. This uses solubility: the toxic oxalate salts are soluble in water and dissolve out of the plant material into the water. Step 2: the soaking is done in running water (e.g. a stream) and the water is repeatedly changed. This creates an open system: the dissolved toxin ions are continually carried away, so the concentration of the toxin in the water stays low and, by Le Châtelier's principle, the dissolving equilibrium $toxin(s)\rightleftharpoons ions(aq)$ is continually pushed to the right until almost all of the toxin has dissolved. The food, with the toxin removed, is then safe to eat (and cooking can also help).

questions.question: Using the data on the data sheet ($K_{sp}(AgCl)=1.77\times10^{-10}$ at $25^\circ$C), quantitatively and qualitatively compare the solubility of silver chloride in water with its solubility in a $0.10$ mol L$^{-1}$ solution of sodium chloride, at $25^\circ$C.
questions.answer: In water: $AgCl(s)\rightleftharpoons Ag^+(aq)+Cl^-(aq)$, $K_{sp}=[Ag^+][Cl^-]=s^2=1.77\times10^{-10}$, so $s=\sqrt{1.77\times10^{-10}}=1.3\times10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$. In $0.10$ M $NaCl$: $[Cl^-]=0.10+s\approx0.10$ M (since $s$ is very small), so $s=\dfrac{K_{sp}}{[Cl^-]}=\dfrac{1.77\times10^{-10}}{0.10}=1.8\times10^{-9}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Comparison: $AgCl$ is much less soluble in the sodium chloride solution (about $7\times10^3$ times less soluble) than in pure water. This is the common ion effect: the added $Cl^-$ shifts the equilibrium to the left, decreasing the solubility.

questions.question: A chemist reacted different volumes of sodium chloride solution with separate $50$ mL samples of silver nitrate solution. After each reaction the silver chloride precipitate was filtered, dried and weighed. The graph shows the mass of precipitate formed against the volume of sodium chloride solution used (mass rises, then is constant at $0.70$ g from $50$ mL to $80$ mL). Explain the shape of the graph from $50$ mL to $80$ mL of sodium chloride used.
questions.answer: From $50$ mL to $80$ mL the graph is flat: the mass of precipitate is constant at about $0.70$ g. By $50$ mL all of the silver nitrate (the limiting reagent) has reacted, so no more $AgCl$ can form however much more sodium chloride is added; the extra sodium chloride is in excess.

questions.question: A chemist reacted different volumes of sodium chloride solution with separate $50$ mL samples of silver nitrate solution: $AgNO_3+NaCl\to AgCl+NaNO_3$. The maximum mass of $AgCl$ precipitate formed was $0.70$ g (reached at $50$ mL of sodium chloride). Calculate the concentration of the silver nitrate solution in mol L$^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
The maximum mass of precipitate is $0.70$ g. $n(AgCl)=\dfrac{0.70}{143.32}=4.88\times10^{-3}$ mol. From the 1:1 ratio, $n(AgNO_3)=4.88\times10^{-3}$ mol, so $c=\dfrac{4.88\times10^{-3}}{0.050}=0.098$ mol L$^{-1}$.

Note: the marking guide gives $0.097$ mol L$^{-1}$; the value is $0.0977$ (0.098 to 2 s.f.), and both were accepted.

questions.question: Two differently coloured complex ions of cobalt(II), $[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ (pink) and $[CoCl_4]^{2-}$ (blue), exist in equilibrium in solution when chloride ions are present: $[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}(aq)+4Cl^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons[CoCl_4]^{2-}(aq)+6H_2O(l)$. Recount how you tested the reversibility of this equilibrium in class.
questions.answer: A piece of filter paper was dipped in the pink cobalt(II) chloride solution and dried over a flame (heating), which turned the paper blue (the equilibrium shifts to the right as water is removed). A drop of water was then added, which turned the paper pink again (the equilibrium shifts to the left), and drying again returned it to blue. This showed that the reaction is reversible and that the colour changes in both directions. (Alternatively, heating and cooling the solution, or adding chloride ions and then water.)

questions.question: An identical cuvette was filled with an aqueous $0.9900$ mol L$^{-1}$ sodium chloride solution and placed in a UV-Vis spectrometer set at a blue wavelength. $[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ was then added so that its initial concentration in the cuvette was $0.3600$ mol L$^{-1}$ (sodium ions play no part in this equilibrium). Account for the use of sodium chloride solution in the cuvette.
questions.answer: The sodium chloride solution is a source of chloride ions, $Cl^-$, which are a reactant. A high concentration of $Cl^-$ pushes the equilibrium to the right (Le Châtelier's principle) to form the blue $[CoCl_4]^{2-}$, producing a measurable absorbance at the blue wavelength. It also keeps $[Cl^-]$ essentially constant and known.

questions.question: Two differently coloured complex ions of cobalt(II) exist in equilibrium: $[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}(aq)+4Cl^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons[CoCl_4]^{2-}(aq)+6H_2O(l)$. A calibration graph (absorbance against $[CoCl_4]^{2-}$) was recorded at a blue wavelength. A cuvette containing $0.9900$ mol L$^{-1}$ $NaCl$ had $[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}$ added to give an initial concentration of $0.3600$ mol L$^{-1}$, and the absorbance rose and levelled off at $0.40$ (graph shown). Calculate $K_{eq}$ for the cobalt(II) complex equilibrium reaction.
questions.answer: At equilibrium the absorbance is $0.40$. From the calibration graph, this corresponds to $[CoCl_4]^{2-}=6\times10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$. By the 1:1:4 stoichiometry, $[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}=0.3600-0.0006=0.3594$ M and $[Cl^-]=0.9900-4(0.0006)=0.9876$ M. Water is omitted from the expression (it is a liquid and its concentration is essentially constant). $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[CoCl_4^{2-}]}{[Co(H_2O)_6^{2+}][Cl^-]^4}=\dfrac{6\times10^{-4}}{0.3594\times(0.9876)^4}=1.75\times10^{-3}$.

questions.question: Information on the reactivity and spectra of an unknown organic compound is given: acidified potassium dichromate added to the sample: orange colour remains; bromine water added to the sample: orange/brown colour remains; sodium carbonate added to the sample: no bubbles. The mass spectrum (molecular ion at $m/z=58$, base peak at $m/z=43$), infrared spectrum, $^{13}$C NMR and $^1$H NMR spectra are shown. Identify the unknown organic compound.
questions.answer: The unknown compound is propanone (acetone).

questions.question: The unknown organic compound is propanone. Draw the structural formula that represents this compound.
questions.answer: $CH_3-C(=O)-CH_3$: a central carbon double-bonded to an oxygen atom and single-bonded to two $CH_3$ groups (all atoms and bonds shown in the full structural formula).

questions.question: Information on the reactivity and spectra of an unknown organic compound is given: acidified potassium dichromate added to the sample: orange colour remains; bromine water added to the sample: orange/brown colour remains; sodium carbonate added to the sample: no bubbles. The mass spectrum, infrared spectrum, $^{13}$C NMR and $^1$H NMR spectra are shown. The compound is propanone. Justify the identification of this compound by referring to the reactivity data and spectra provided.
questions.answer: **Reactivity tests.** Acidified dichromate stays orange, so the compound is not a primary or secondary alcohol or an aldehyde (it could be a tertiary alcohol or a ketone). Bromine water stays orange/brown, so there is no $C=C$ or $C\equiv C$ bond (it is saturated). Sodium carbonate gives no bubbles, so there is no carboxylic acid. **Mass spectrum.** The molecular ion peak is at $m/z=58$ (the small peak at 59 is due to a $^{13}C$ isotope), so the molar mass is 58 g mol$^{-1}$, which fits $C_3H_6O$ ($3\times12.01+6\times1.008+16.00=58.08$). The peak at 43 is the $CH_3CO^+$ fragment (and 15 is $CH_3^+$). **Infrared spectrum.** A strong, sharp absorption at about $1700$ cm$^{-1}$ is a carbonyl ($C=O$) group (aldehyde or ketone), and the weaker absorption at about $3000$ cm$^{-1}$ is $C-H$. There is no broad absorption above $2500$ cm$^{-1}$, so there is no $O-H$ or $COOH$ group, which confirms the chemical tests. **$^{13}$C NMR.** There are two carbon environments for the three carbons, so two carbons must be equivalent (symmetry). The peak at about $30$ ppm is an $R-CH_3$ carbon (within the $5$–$40$ ppm range) and the peak at about $200+$ ppm is a ketone/aldehyde carbonyl carbon ($190$–$220$ ppm). **$^1$H NMR.** There is one signal (a singlet) at about $2.1$ ppm, so all hydrogens are equivalent. It is a singlet, so the neighbouring carbon has no hydrogens (n + 1 rule, $0+1=1$), i.e. the two $CH_3$ groups are attached to the carbonyl carbon, with no $-CHO$ aldehyde hydrogen (which would appear at about $9$–$10$ ppm). A symmetrical ketone with mass 58 is propanone, $CH_3COCH_3$.
